<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>User namespaces + file capabilities = trouble</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103429/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103429/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description><a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/532593/">User namespaces</a> are a key part of the
kernel's toolkit for assembling containers; processes within a user
namespace can appear to have full root access to the system while gaining
no extra privileges in the wider system.  At least, that is the intent.  In
practice, keeping privilege contained within a user namespace has often
turned out to be difficult.  As an example, consider <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20261027-b4-setfcap-userns-v8-0-2674adc63f3c@toxicpanda.com">this
small patch series</a> from Josef Bacik, which is intended to address some
situations where a process within a user namespace can elevate the
privileges of processes outside of it.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Locking down hibernation for the winter</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103190/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103190/</guid>
			<dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
			<description><p>
When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and
then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data
back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off.
Unfortunately, the kernel does not have
any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with,
which is why <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/791863/">lockdown</a>, an optional kernel
feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation.
Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared
<a href="https://lwn.net/ml/linux-pm/20261008132532.1155166-1-matthewg@nvidia.com/">
a patch set</a> that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect
against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older
kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.
</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Git considers voting to determine its LLM policy</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1104195/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1104195/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>One of the dominant themes of 2026 has been the debate within development
projects about the terms under which LLM-written contributions should be
accepted — if, indeed, they should be accepted at all.  The <a
href="https://git-scm.com/">Git project</a> has not been immune to this
trend; the topic was <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/summit-2026.94e33e9ddf234334.06@ttaylorr.com">discussed</a>
at the recent Git Contributor's Summit.  In this case, the path to a
resolution may be somewhat circuitous; the project, which has never been
governed as a democracy, is considering adopting a voting process as a way
of bringing the discussion to an acceptable conclusion.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102549/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102549/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p>Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a <a
href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DisplayLink">DisplayLink</a> chipset
that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He
decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one
problem that he could not solve&mdash;so he asked for help, hoping that
Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was <a
href="https://www.synaptics.com/company/news/displaylink">acquired by
Synaptics</a> in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the
driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement
claims, a <a
href="https://lists.freedesktop.org/archives/dri-devel/attachments/20261006/d690bb16/attachment-0001.pdf">demand</a>
that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats
of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the
company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other
platforms.</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Additional hardening for the glibc dynamic linker</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1105134/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1105134/</guid>
			<dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
			<description><p>
The
<a href="https://nodejs.org/en">
Node.js project</a> recently had a
<a href="https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/october-2026-security-releases#nodejs-brotli-decoder-out-of-bounds-write-permits-remote-code-execution-cve-2026-111497---high">
security vulnerability</a> that
affected its
<a href="https://brotli.org/">
Brotli</a> decoder. The bug
<a href="https://project-zero.issues.chromium.org/issues/565308158">
was a buffer overflow</a>,
but the particular way that official Node.js binaries are built for Linux meant that one of the
main protections against turning a buffer overflow into remote code execution,
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Address_space_layout_randomization">
address space layout randomization</a> (ASLR) could not be turned on. If ASLR had been
enabled, the bug would still be exploitable in theory, but much more difficult
to exploit in practice. In response, the GNU C Library (glibc) is
<a href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20261028175613.3779425-1-adhemerval.zanella@linaro.org/">
considering</a> a new set of
<a href="https://sourceware.org/glibc/manual/latest/html_node/Tunables.html">
tunable settings</a> to allow administrators to forbid programs that do not
support ASLR. The new settings, while a welcome hardening measure, may not
address the root problem.
</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>C++26 contract confusion</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1105400/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1105400/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
The
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organization_for_Standardization">
International Organization for Standardization</a> (ISO) has blessed seven C++
language revisions since 1998.
The language is mostly developed by ISO's
<a href="https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/">
Working Group 21</a>, which
considers proposed additions and amendments, integrates them into a document,
and then presents that document to the main ISO body to be voted on as a
standard. On October&#160;23, for the first time ever, ISO declined to ratify a document
presented by Working Group 21, leaving the future of the C++26 standard in
doubt. The decision was driven by controversy around a proposed new "contracts"
feature that would add pre- and post-conditions to function signatures.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 03 Dec 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>25 years of Buildroot</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103395/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103395/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description><a href="https://buildroot.org/">Buildroot</a> maintainer Peter Korsgaard
gave a <a href="https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/f9c6efe062af6ec8de28f2b67b84e112">presentation</a> about the long history of the build tool for embedded
Linux systems at the 2026 <a
href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/embedded-linux-conference-europe/">Embedded
Linux Conference Europe</a>.  In it, he covered more than just the past 25
years, looking at the current status of the project as well as what to
expect in Buildroot's future. It was an interesting view inside this long-running project that
has been a mainstay of the embedded-Linux world throughout almost all of
this century.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 03 Dec 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>A new generation of futexes</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102988/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102988/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description><a href="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/futex.7.html">Futexes</a>
are a kernel subsystem that provides support for fast mutexes
in user space.  While futexes can indeed be fast, they are not fast enough
for a number of users.  Partly as a result of that, the implementation of
futexes has grown in complexity over the years, with two basic variants
on offer.  The desire for faster futexes remains, though, and that inspires
new patches, including <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260917043339.2093426-1-suleiman@google.com">this series
from Suleiman Souhlal</a> adding a third futex class called "futex PING"
for "priority inheritance next generation".
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 03 Dec 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Zellij manages terminal workspaces with style</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1106913/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1106913/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p><a href="https://zellij.dev">Zellij</a> is a relatively new entrant in the
<a
href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_multiplexer">terminal-multiplexer</a>
category. Like <a href="https://www.gnu.org/software/screen/">GNU
Screen</a> and <a href="https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki">tmux</a> it gives
users the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes,
provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for
browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely
more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, <a
href="https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij/releases/tag/v0.46.0">version&#160;0.46</a>,
adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings
screen so users can configure the application without fussing with
configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not
yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to
meet the needs of many users.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 03 Dec 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Julia 1.13 brings REPL improvements and more</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1108153/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1108153/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>Version&#160;1.13 of <a href="https://julialang.org/">Julia</a> was <a
href="https://julialang.org/blog/2026/09/julia-1.13-highlights/index.html">released</a>
on September 10, 2026. Julia is a general-purpose language especially well
suited to high-performance numerical computing. Its expressiveness, speed, and <a href="https://arstechnica.com/science/2020/10/the-unreasonable-effectiveness-of-the-julia-programming-language/">composability</a> have made it increasingly popular with scientists and mathematicians.
We last looked at Julia <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1044280/">one year ago</a>, in a
review of the 1.12&#160;release. The newest version features an enhanced
read-eval-print loop (REPL), a GUI for installation, a smoother developer experience, and an assortment of performance improvements.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 03 Dec 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Added indirection allows for larger BPF programs</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1106537/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1106537/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of
execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety
properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the
number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow.
Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared
<a href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20261105204513.2230344-1-alexei.starovoitov@gmail.com/">
a patch set</a> that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in
order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Dec 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Bringing the Agama installer to openSUSE Tumbleweed</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1107830/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1107830/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>The <a href="https://opensuse.org/">openSUSE Project</a> has been working on
the <a href="https://agama-project.github.io/">Agama installer</a> for four
years; it was the default installer for <a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1019688/">openSUSE&#160;Leap&#160;16.0</a> when
it was released in 2025, and has been adopted by other openSUSE flavors as
well. Now the project is gearing up to go all-in on Agama for <a
href="https://get.opensuse.org/tumbleweed/">Tumbleweed</a>, the rolling-release
edition that is meant to be where updates and new features land first. Even so,
the community has concerns about losing some of <a
href="https://yast.opensuse.org/">YaST's</a> legacy functionality and
the impact on installing Tumbleweed on systems that have less RAM.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 10 Dec 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
